## Abstract

Artificial intelligence (AI) provides an opportunity to streamline tasks within academic medicine. Generative AI (genAI) models, specifically, have the capacity to generate new written content, follow detailed instructions for product improvement, and incorporate content from supplemental data sources. While a part of the professional responsibility of faculty in academic medicine, writing letters of recommendation (LORs) is often time consuming and repetitive candidate to candidate. Yet, crafting these letters well is paramount to convey an applicant’s unique attributes in a time when pass/fail grading and remote interviews are increasingly common.

In this article, the authors provide an approachable framework for the ethical use of genAI to assist with writing LORs in academic medicine. They briefly discuss the fundamental structure of genAI, the advantages between several genAI models specifically for the task of letter writing, privacy concerns that can develop when using genAI, iterative methods to develop effective prompts to craft letter drafts, personalization of finalized content, genAI use to identify bias, and appropriate documentation of AI usage.

Once practiced, this process can prevent the need for shortcuts, such as copying and pasting from CVs or re-using previously written letters between candidates, that currently sacrifice letter quality to reduce writing time. Ethical use, privacy, and disclosure necessitate a deliberate framework for the use of genAI in letter writing. Future research is needed to inform the development of a specific AI model to generate LORs. The framework presented here provides faculty with the steps needed to begin incorporating genAI into their letter writing practice.

Since initial conceptions of artificial intelligence (AI), skeptics have postulated AI would perpetually be limited in its ability to rival the creativity and complexity of the human mind.1 Today, the AI frontier has advanced far beyond these expectations.2,3 Within the academic medicine and scientific professions, people have used generative AI (genAI) to write clinical medical records,4 craft personal statements,5 evaluate learners,6,7 revise primary research articles,8 and collate and summarize literature findings.8 GenAI is particularly helpful to humans in completing tasks that generate new content while following instructions and incorporating facts from supplemental data sources.3

A career in academic medicine requires faculty to collaborate with, advocate for, and promote trainees and colleagues during their professional growth. As such, we are often called to write letters of recommendation (LORs) to support our trainees’ and colleagues’ applications to formal training programs, award or grant candidacy, and academic promotion. At a time when standardized tests and professional education programs are moving to pass/fail grading and many interviews are now remote encounters,9 the stalwart LOR remains one of the few robust, holistic metrics for in-depth insight into the character and quality of the applicant.10

However, the LOR faces several challenges, key among them the inordinately time-consuming nature of crafting a high-quality, candidate-specific letter.11 Likely our ideals for ourselves as letter writers are often not realized; we are often shoehorning this task into our otherwise stuffed schedules of competing demands. Thus, we may take shortcuts, using previously written LORs as templates to be modified from one candidate to the next, cutting and pasting from the documents provided by the candidate, and writing and submitting quickly to meet deadlines.11 When not crafted exceedingly well, LORs can perpetuate harm, particularly to disadvantaged groups.10 Multiple studies have shown that there is pervasive racial and gender bias specifically in LORs in academic medicine.10,12,13 Interventions to date to correct this bias have been insufficient to solve the problem.14,15

GenAI, when utilized well, has the potential to improve the writing experience for mentors and simultaneously developing stronger letters unique to each candidate while minimizing bias. In a small study comparing letters of support for promotion, human reviewers were unable to distinguish between human- versus AI-authored letters.16 As medical education leaders and scientific mentors, each of us on this authorship team writes many LORs each year, often all within the same month during specific application seasons. Here, we outline our framework for utilizing genAI to write our LORs, informed initially by literature developed in the informatics and business sectors and refined for medical trainees through our own practical experience using this technology over the last year. Our structured framework described below has allowed our team to reduce our writing steps and time while maintaining our style, tone, and desired level of candidate recommendation.

While the academic medicine and scientific communities have discussed guidelines for the ethical use of genAI in research methodologies and scientific writing,17,18 we as a profession have yet to critically examine how AI might best be used and disclosed in the LOR writing process. Though not yet formally studied, we provide our method to inform today’s safe use of genAI to write LORs in academic medicine, addressing technical functionalities, an iterative improvement process, and the unique challenges that can arise.

## Choosing a GenAI Model

GenAI is a form of AI that creates new content. For example, large language models (LLMs) are a type of genAI that specializes in text generation; these models are trained on vast data sets to predict the next word or sentence in a text sequence.19 Popular LLMs such as ChatGPT 3.5 (OpenAI), Gemini (Google), and Claude (Anthropic) are general-purpose models that excel at generating text and have easy to use chat interfaces that allow the user to interact conversationally with the platform.19,20 Meta’s LLaMA (Large Language Model Meta AI) also excels at text generation but is distinct due to its efficiency, lower resource requirements, and non-commercial license.21 LLMs can also be integrated into other software. For instance, Microsoft 365 Copilot combines OpenAI’s GPT models with Microsoft Office applications, allowing users to generate drafts or assist with revisions directly in Word.22

All these LLMs are suitable for drafting and revising LORs. Given the AI-generated LOR privacy concerns we address in the next section, the choice of which model to use may already be made for a faculty member if their institution has developed and encourages the use of enterprise-grade information security protections within a specific LLM product.

## Addressing Privacy Concerns

Since its creation, genAI has come under scrutiny for privacy concerns.23 Researchers have discovered that personally identifiable data have been distributed in genAI training data sets.24 Interaction data and user prompts are often saved locally and can be accessed in the event of a cyberbreach.24 Even without malicious intent, genAI models have been known to store and regurgitate personal information when prompted, raising concern that any data used in a genAI setting fundamentally can no longer be considered private.25 While countries have begun instituting protections to address these flaws and meet data security and consumer privacy expectations, privacy when using such technology is not guaranteed.26

We strongly recommend that individuals work with their institution to review policies, guidance, and tools for using LLMs for personally identifiable information. Some institutions have created specialized LLM environments or “sandboxes” that enable employees to access LLMs in a secure environment.27 Using these environments, faculty will be able to create LORs that include personal information without concern for sharing the data with the LLMs or vendors. If an institution lacks a secure environment, faculty should consult institutional leadership to explore safe LLM options. Faculty also can consider using secure health care-focused LLMs like Doximity’s GPT28 but should still review privacy and data sharing terms closely. They should avoid using public LLMs without strict data-sharing restrictions, as even de-identified sensitive content may carry re-identification risks.29

## Choosing an Approach

Writing in any form is best done iteratively, and this is particularly important when writing with AI.30 GenAI should be seen as an assistant to the writer, but it cannot and should not replace the human component. An effective LOR writer needs to convey both the relationship they have with the applicant and the personal, humanizing aspects of that person.31 The question is how to best intermingle the human and AI contributions. In our experience, there are 2 main approaches that we have termed AI-as-editor and AI-as-author.

In the AI-as-editor approach, we write the letter ourselves in the traditional manner, adding aspects of the applicant’s resume and personal anecdotes about their performance. We then ask the AI to revise the letter with very specific instructions on what aspect(s) needs improvement. For example, we can ask the AI to elevate the central tone to impart the relationship with the applicant or to highlight certain themes and strengths. The primary benefit of the AI-as-editor option is that it is closer to the classic method of writing LORs and is akin to sending the letter to another collaborator for revision. We think this method would be best suited to individuals who have an established protocol for writing LORs and are hoping to incorporate AI for a specific task, such as to minimize bias or improve the clarity, standardization, and impact of their letters.

The AI-as-author approach, which may appear complicated at first, has the potential to dramatically increase efficiency and improve standardization for those who write many letters. In this process, we use a series of prompts to focus the text that AI produces in different portions of the letter in an iterative manner, integrating the human component throughout and improving cohesion of the piece.30

Both AI-as-editor and AI-as-author have benefits, which we use to decide which approach is best depending on our relationship with the applicant. For example, for candidates we know well, we typically use the AI-as-editor approach, creating a human-derived first draft focusing on our many specific personal experiences with and feedback on the candidate. Meanwhile, we find the AI-as-author approach to work well for candidates we do not know well personally, such as when serving as outside “at arm’s length” reviewers for colleagues up for academic promotion for whom we are objectively reviewing a resume only, without the luxury of a professional relationship with the candidate.

## The Process of Prompt Engineering

While genAI can create sophisticated content, its ability to generate material that is fully aligned with the desire of the user is largely determined by the human prompt or the input to the LLM. Prompts can be deconstructed into 4 fundamental components: instruction, context, the input data, and the output indicator.32 Instruction describes the specific task one desires the model to perform. Context provides external information about why and to what purpose this prompt is being submitted and can be important for improving applicability to the scenario at hand. Input data represents the scenario for which the user wishes to receive an answer, and the output indicator is simply the format of the desired final output.32

Prompt engineering is the practice of iteratively designing the input to LLMs to elicit desired and accurate responses.33,34 For example, consider the task of writing a LOR for an associate professor at another institution who is applying for tenure at her school. Our prompt in this situation could be: I am an Associate Professor of [specialty] at [school name] with [x] years of experience in [field] and have worked with [applicant name] for the past [y] years as a collaborator on [project]. Write a letter of recommendation for [applicant name] to support her promotion from Assistant Professor to Associate Professor that should convey she is a national expert in [specific field]. The instruction is inherent in “write a letter of recommendation” and provides the output indicator (LOR). The context for this prompt is the first sentence naming the relationship between the writer and the applicant. Other content we may provide includes specific information, such as the promotion criteria at the candidate’s home institution or the candidate’s CV. The input data can be found in the latter half of the second sentence in which we convey the specific scenario under scrutiny, namely the promotion from assistant professor to associate professor. ## Developing the Letter

We start by opening a new interface chat session to ensure the model does not accidently insert any erroneous information from any previous genAI tasks. To begin, we recommend breaking the letter-writing process into several smaller subtasks.33 Such subtasks include constructing the LOR structure (as exemplified in the prompt engineering section above), crafting the letter’s message, outlining the key points, adding details, quantifying skill, and modifying the tone. Example prompts to complete these tasks for writing a LOR for faculty promotion can be found in Figure 1. This will generate the first iteration of the letter.

Instructions should guide the genAI model to focus the letter on a particular message,34 which we refine or highlight in next drafts. The prompt should stress a particular angle that should be emphasized about the quality of the candidate, such as their clinical or research prowess, empathetic or decisive manner, or extensive work experience in the field. Being detailed and transparent regarding the intended message will ensure this specific, desired messaging will be featured prominently throughout the suggested text and will make the letter more impactful.34 We can combine this step with instructions that detail a desired outline of the letter structure by guiding the model to focus on specific aspects of the candidate’s resume and experience that would appeal to the letter reader. For example, for a medical student applying to residency, we can instruct the model to “include a paragraph dedicated to their clinical experience and talents, a second paragraph dedicated to their research, and a third paragraph dedicated to their prior work in education.” We can prompt the genAI model “to emphasize throughout the letter their team-building and problem-solving attributes” or “incorporate throughout the letter their interest in mentorship of women and underrepresented minority colleagues.”

We then add details from the applicant’s CV or other documents to flesh out the LOR specifically for this candidate. To do so, we manually create a list of key accomplishments from their CV or copy and paste relevant content from their CV into the LLM. Some LLM interfaces, such as Microsoft Office 365 Copilot, have an option for uploading documents.

Lastly, we tailor the letter to suit our chosen level of recommendation.31,35 Perhaps the most important instruction to provide upfront is to include a statement regarding the quality of the candidate in the letter, which may describe how this candidate compares to others we have worked with.36 Language such as “top 10%,” “top 1%,” “one of the top 5 students in my class,” or “the best researcher I have ever worked with” are much more useful than superlatives such as “excellent,” “great,” or “good” that can have different meanings for different writers and different readers.36 We often include in quotes specific descriptions of how our home institution views this candidate (e.g., “will be actively recruiting this applicant,” “are excited to see their career grow,” or “will be a welcome addition to any program”). If specific language, such as percentiles, is desired, we explicitly tell the model to include it.

Once we have organized our materials and prompts for the model, the development of the initial draft takes just a few seconds. However, this truly is a process of iterative refinement, and we never use a first draft as the final draft. The most common stumbling block we find in this letter development process is that the text the genAI produces is close to what we want to convey but not quite exact. We then further refine the letter either with the human-as-editor approach to edit to the exact language and message we want, or we can be very specific with the next genAI text prompt, inserting the prior text and telling it with as much specificity as possible how the text should be changed in the next draft. This latter method may need to be repeated several times.

## Crafting Tone and Personalizing the Letter

The more detailed the context we provide to the genAI model, the more relevant and helpful the final product will be.34 This extends to providing information about us as the author, such as how long we have known the applicant and from what perspective we will be attesting to their potential.36

We can create the tone we desire through several strategies.37 One is to directly guide the model to craft the content in a certain voice (e.g., more “formal,” “conversational,” “sophisticated”). GenAI can go so far as to write the letter in the voice of a specific person or professional role.37 We have used this function by asking the program to draft the letter as if it was written “by the CEO of a pharmaceutical company” for an applicant to a science leadership position or “by a U.S. Senator” for a veteran student applying into a military residency. Similarly, once a first draft of the letter is created (either by the author or by AI), in the next prompt, we state what is wrong with the current tone and content of the letter and give the program specific instructions on how to fix it. This allows the model to iterate on the content.30 Another option for specifying tone is to provide the model with previous writing samples in the desired voice, which would be our previous human-derived letters.37

The last step in customizing this letter requires us to incorporate personal anecdotes or feedback quotations about the candidate.36 These stories and quotations often are the key to composing a memorable LOR and provide priceless insight into the core components of the candidate’s qualities that cannot be conveyed by academic accomplishments alone. Furthermore, including these features highlights our relationship to the applicant and strengthens our unique authority to testify to their talents. This step is likely heavily or solely human-derived regardless of our chosen approach thus far (AI-as-author or AI-as-editor).

## Minimizing Bias

It has been well established that LORs remain fraught with racial and gender bias. Human-derived LORs for women and racial minority applicants are more likely to emphasize their effort and personal characteristics rather than their accomplishments.10,38,39

Using genAI affords us an opportunity to correct this bias by improving standardization across letters and bringing awareness to any differences in applicant descriptors between letters. In a single-masked quasi-experimental study where academic physicians reviewed LORs written by either humans or AI, human-authored letters contained significantly more female-associated words, while the majority of AI-authored letters used more male-associated words.16

Even for faculty who feel strongly about writing their own LOR from salutation to signature, we recommend they ask genAI as a final step to deliberately probe their letter for potential bias. For example, we ask genAI the following questions: “How many agentic adjectives appear in this LOR?” “How many communal adjectives appear?” “How many publications are mentioned in this letter?” and “Does this letter emphasize accomplishments or effort more?” While current genAI models still struggle to identify some of these particular features, using them in combination with other resources, such as agentic language databases, shows significant promise.40 Once unintentional bias is identified, we rebalance the text to fix it.

Although a promising resource, genAI itself can be biased towards or against certain groups simply due to it being trained using human-derived data, thus amplifying any human-derived bias in those data.41 OpenAI has tackled this from the user end, harnessing humans to provide feedback on ChatGPT responses and then using that feedback to retrain their model, a technique that is still prone to bias by virtue of the continued use of humans in the retraining process.42 Google has been accused of introducing counter bias in its efforts to retrain Gemini on the front end, generating controversy over its racially inaccurate portrayals of historically prominent figures and highly one-sided perspectives on political topics.43 However, one of the benefits of using AI in letter writing is that the gender, race, and other identifiers of the applicant can be masked to the program, helping to reduce some of the bias inherent in a human author.

## Documenting Usage

While many are still in the process of drafting precise guidelines for how to disclose the use of genAI in writing, most institutions agree that some sort of disclosure should occur.44,45 As the role of genAI in writing will likely expand, we agree that it is important to set documentation standards early. Before we started using AI to assist in writing LORs, we investigated our institution’s own policy, and we watch for changes at our institution regarding AI use and disclosure.46

Next, when we are approached to write a LOR, we vary our disclosure to the letter requestor depending on the position of the person making the request. If the candidate themself asks for a letter, part of our initial conversation with them is to discuss the strength of the letter we can write for them and the documents we need to assist in the letter writing. During this conversation, we also inform the candidate that we currently use genAI to assist in all our writing to streamline the process, correct grammar, and mitigate bias but that we guarantee the content and assertions will be ours alone and will appropriately express our recommendation of them as a candidate. If we are asked to write a LOR from a third party, such as a department chair for an arms-length letter for academic promotion, we do not disclose our planned use of AI when we agree to write the letter; instead we include the disclosure (see below) in the letter itself. This is our personal practice. We could find no guidance from experts in ethical writing or published guidelines in the current literature to inform our practice.

We advise everyone to include their use of genAI in the LORs themselves in preparation for more stringent disclosure guidelines and for normalization of the use of genAI, both of which we believe are likely ahead. We accomplish this disclosure in a final, short paragraph at the end of the letter. With the concern that acknowledging this usage may potentially bias evaluators against these letters,47 we do this in a way that normalizes our use of AI to avoid any one letter being “flagged” as inauthentic. Lastly, we use this documentation to make it clear that we, the human signing the letter, ultimately take full responsibility for the content.

An example of our disclosure is: I use AI to assist in writing all my letters of recommendation and do so because I believe it creates a better reflection of my thoughts on each applicant. Portions of this letter were written in conjunction with the assistance of [AI program] to ensure consistency of letter tone and content specific to [applicant name] and for minimization of unconscious bias. All AI-generated portions have been reviewed and checked for accuracy by me as the undersigned.

## Reviewing the Final Product

GenAI, while highly promising, must be used with an awareness of its limitations and potential harms. These programs have shown a concerning inability to discern fact from fiction, repeating inaccurate information from the internet or even creating fictional content.48,49 Therefore, it is essential that human authors review all content and confirm the validity and unbiased nature of any AI produced text. As with any writing, we highly recommend a last step to scrutinize the final product for such errors. It is in this final editing phase where we add in identifying information, such as applicant name, institutional names, and other sensitive information if we deliberately kept it from the model given the above privacy concerns.

## Current Limitations and Future Opportunities

The recommendations we provide here are primarily based on our experience and the informatics and business literature. There is a significant need for rigorous, quantitative research to determine the most effective strategies for using LLMs in drafting LORs for a wide variety of candidates and application types. Specifically, comparative studies are required to evaluate the performance and cost-effectiveness of various LLMs in the context of LOR generation. Further research should also focus on optimizing prompt engineering to maximize the quality and relevance of generated content.

As the field matures, there is potential to develop a specialized, user-friendly AI assistant for LORs that systematically guides users through inputting candidate information and evaluations and utilizes optimized prompts to generate high-quality recommendations. Research into the costs and the cost savings in training people on these AI-assistants will also be needed.

We do recognize that people hold varying degrees of eagerness to adopt a new technology, and several sociotechnical factors across individual, technical, organizational, and regulator domains may influence a person’s willingness to use AI for writing letters of recommendation.50 For example, some individuals may lack trust in the accuracy or appropriateness of AI-generated content, while others may avoid AI due to unfamiliarity or perceived technical complexity. Additional investigation is needed to fully understand and address these barriers.

## Conclusion

GenAI has the potential to maximize benefits to both letter writers and applicants, creating a win-win scenario by automating administrative tasks while also reducing unconscious bias and elevating the impact of a letter’s message. There are suitable approaches for all individuals regardless of technological prowess. For beginners, genAI can be a great tool to revise already written letters and, for the most advanced, it can be a transformative technique for streamlining the whole letter writing process. Furthermore, by standardizing our approach to identifying and correcting unconscious bias in letter writing, genAI boosts our ability to create a fair application process. We encourage all in academic medicine to explore the potentials of AI in their own letter writing, and we are excited to see how this may benefit the promotion of our trainees and faculty colleagues alike.
